The town had a museum for things nobody thought to save. It occupied the old post office, between a bakery and a shop that sold batteries. There were no paintings on its walls. Instead, glass cases held a single blue button, a chipped teaspoon, a paper ticket to a cinema that had closed before I was born. Every object had a label explaining who had brought it and what they remembered. The museum charged no admission. Most days, nobody went in.

I started visiting during the summer I was meant to leave town. My train ticket was booked for September, and I had a list of practical things to do: sell my bicycle, pack my clothes, call the landlord about a leak. Instead, I spent afternoons reading labels. The button had come from a winter coat worn by three sisters in turn. The teaspoon had belonged to a man who stirred every cup of tea exactly seven times. Someone had kept the cinema ticket because it was the first time she had gone anywhere alone.

At the back of the museum, behind a curtain, was a room without cases. Shelves held hundreds of small cardboard boxes. A handwritten sign said **SOUNDS**, though the boxes appeared empty. I lifted the lid of one marked *Front gate, 1986* and heard a metal latch click, followed by footsteps hurrying across gravel. I nearly dropped it. When I opened it again, the same footsteps crossed the same gravel.

The curator found me standing there with the lid in my hands. Her name was Mrs. Vale, and she was old enough that people had begun describing her as if she were a historic building. She said the boxes worked only for sounds someone had loved enough to remember clearly. She did not know why. Her predecessor had discovered the first one decades ago, after placing an empty box beside his bed to catch a mouse. In the morning, it contained his mother singing while she washed dishes.

I asked whether anyone could make one. Mrs. Vale handed me a box and told me to try. I thought of the leak in my apartment, but all I heard was my own breathing. I thought of the bakery bell, which rang each time the door opened, and heard nothing. Then I remembered my father knocking twice on my bedroom door before entering. For a moment, two firm taps sounded inside the box. They were quieter than I expected, but unmistakable.

My father was alive, only three streets away. Still, I carried the box home in both hands. I had not lived with him for years, and I could no longer recall when his knock had stopped being part of my days. That evening I found him repairing a chair at his kitchen table. I told him about the museum. He laughed, asked whether Mrs. Vale had finally persuaded someone else to dust the shelves, and offered me the chair once its leg was sound.

Over the next few weeks, I helped at the museum. People arrived with memories they wanted to put in boxes: a dog’s paws crossing a wooden floor, rain on a particular roof, the uneven whistle of a kettle long since thrown away. Mrs. Vale showed them how to sit quietly and pay attention. Often they left disappointed. Remembering that a sound existed was not the same as hearing it again in your mind. Some returned the next day with better luck. Others brought photographs or stories instead.

One morning a little boy came in with his grandfather. They had spent the weekend trying to remember the grandmother’s laugh. Both knew it had been loud. The boy said she sometimes laughed so hard she covered her face; his grandfather said she never did. They went back and forth, correcting each other, until the boy grew upset. Mrs. Vale gave them tea and suggested they come back another time. As they were leaving, the grandfather remembered how she used to clear her throat before telling a joke. The boy remembered that too. They made a box for it together.

Near the end of August, I packed the last of my things. The bicycle went to a neighbor’s daughter. My father kept the chair and lent me a suitcase whose wheels pulled stubbornly to the left. On my final day, I returned the box with his knock to the museum. I had listened to it often enough to notice a faint sound after the second tap: my younger self calling, “Come in.” I had forgotten that part. I showed Mrs. Vale the label I had written, and she found it a place on the shelf.

The museum did not make leaving harder. If anything, those weeks had taught me that a town could remain itself without my standing in it. People would keep opening the bakery door and buying batteries. My father would find another chair to repair. Perhaps someone would come looking for the sound of the train as it left the station, though I doubted they would need a box to remember it while trains still ran every day.

On the platform, I heard my father call my name and turned. He had come to return a book I had left in his kitchen. I put it in the crooked suitcase. Then the train arrived, with brakes that squealed all along the platform, and we said goodbye over the noise. Once I had found my seat, I opened the book. Tucked between its pages was a note in his handwriting: *You can always come in.* I read it twice before the train pulled away.
